courses.title: Hazmat Awareness — Recertification
courses.summary: Recognize, isolate, and notify. Refresh your decision frame for hazardous-materials incidents.
courses.credibility: Built with NFPA 472 alignment and reviewed by 3 fire-service SMEs.

blocks.title: Field signs & placards
The first 60 seconds are for reading, not doing
blocks.body: You roll up on a tractor-trailer canted into the ditch, a thin haze drifting off the trailer, a driver waving from the shoulder. Everything in you wants to move. Don't — not yet. Your first job on a hazmat scene is recognition: building an accurate picture of what you're facing before you commit a single step. The placard, the container shape, and what bystanders tell you are three independent signals. Read together from a distance, they tell you whether this is a flammable liquid, a corrosive, a toxic gas, or something that will hurt you long before you smell it. Get the picture wrong and every action after it is wrong too.

blocks.title: What the placard is actually telling you
blocks.body: A DOT placard is a 10-and-3/4-inch diamond that encodes three things at a glance: a color, a hazard class number in the bottom corner, and often a four-digit UN/NA identification number in the center. Color is your fastest read — red means flammable, green non-flammable gas, orange explosive, yellow oxidizer, white poison/inhalation hazard, white-over-black corrosive. The class number (1 through 9) refines it. The UN number names the specific material: 1203 is gasoline, 1017 is chlorine, 1075 is petroleum/LP gas. You don't memorize the catalog — you read the number through binoculars, stay upwind and uphill, and look it up in the Emergency Response Guidebook before you close the distance.

items.title: Color = hazard family
items.body: Red flammable, green non-flammable gas, yellow oxidizer, white poison, white-over-black corrosive. Color is the read you can make from 300 feet.

items.title: Number = the specifics
items.body: The class digit narrows the family; the four-digit UN number names the exact product so the ERG can guide your isolation distances.

items.title: Shape backs it up
items.body: MC-306 ovals carry fuel, MC-331 bullet tanks carry pressurized gas, MC-307 rounded tanks carry chemicals. Shape confirms the placard.

data.label: Placard obscured by damage, soot, or angle
No binoculars used / too close before ID
Wrong or outdated placard on load

blocks.title: What stops responders from reading a placard cleanly
blocks.note: Illustrative distribution drawn from common after-action themes, not a single dataset.

blocks.text: If you can read the placard with your naked eye, you're already standing where the vapor cloud wants you.

blocks.title: Red flags — stop and reassess
items: A placard and the container shape disagree (e.g., a corrosive placard on a pressurized bullet tank).
No placard at all on a vehicle that clearly should have one — assume worst case until proven otherwise.
Pooling liquid, hissing, vapor, frost on a tank, or dead vegetation/insects near the source.
Bystanders or the driver reporting symptoms: burning eyes, difficulty breathing, dizziness.
You cannot read the UN number — do not move closer to read it; reposition and use optics.

blocks.title: Three signals, cross-checked
blocks.body: No single signal is trusted alone. A placard can be wrong — placed for the previous load, knocked loose, or scorched unreadable. Container shape is harder to fake: a high-pressure MC-331 bullet tank doesn't carry diesel, and a non-pressure MC-306 oval doesn't carry chlorine. Bystander reports add the human layer the metal can't — what they saw spill, what they smell, who's already symptomatic. When all three agree, your confidence is high. When they conflict, the conflict itself is the warning: treat the scene as the most dangerous plausible interpretation and verify from a safe stand-off before you revise downward.

blocks.title: The mistakes that close the distance too fast
blocks.body: The recurring error isn't misreading a number — it's skipping the read entirely because the scene looks routine. A fender-bender with a delivery truck still gets the placard check. Responders also anchor on the first label they spot and stop looking, missing a second placard on the opposite side or a shipping-paper detail that changes the class. And they drive in to confirm what binoculars would have told them from safety. Slow is smooth; the picture you build at 300 feet keeps you out of the 30-foot mistakes.

items.body: Position upwind, uphill, and upstream. Park well back and resist the pull to roll closer.
Use binoculars to capture the placard color, class number, and four-digit UN number from a distance.
Match the container or tank profile against the placard. Note any disagreement as a red flag.
Question the driver and bystanders from a safe distance — what spilled, what they smell, who feels sick.
Cross-reference the UN number in the ERG for initial isolation and protective-action distances before acting.

blocks.title: Run the recognition sequence in order
Recognition is the decision
blocks.body: Everything downstream — isolation, evacuation, who you notify — flows from the picture you build in the opening minute. You're not memorizing every chemical on the road; you're training your eye to read color, number, and shape from a safe stand-off and to treat disagreement as danger. Recognize first. Act second. The responders who go home are the ones who spent their first 60 seconds looking.

blocks.prompt: You see a diamond placard with the number 1203 on a tanker. What does that suggest?

options.label: Gasoline (flammable liquid)
options.feedback: Correct — UN 1203 is gasoline. Your isolation distance defaults to 50m and grows with fire involvement.

options.label: Corrosive liquid
options.feedback: Not quite — corrosives use class 8 placards, not UN 1203.

options.label: Compressed oxygen
options.feedback: Oxygen is UN 1072 with a class 2.2 (oxidizer) placard.

blocks.title: Wind, slope, and the 50m rule
The perimeter is alive
blocks.body: On arrival, isolation is not a number you set once and forget. It is a living distance. It expands the instant you see vapor, feel heat, or watch a bystander cough, stagger, or rub their eyes. It contracts only after monitoring confirms the air is clean. Your first job at a hazmat scene is not identification, decon, or rescue. It is to draw a line, keep people behind it, and be willing to move that line outward the moment the scene tells you to. Everything else fails if the perimeter fails.

blocks.title: Fifty meters is the floor, not the answer
blocks.body: Treat 50 meters as the absolute minimum for any small spill or unidentified container — the distance that keeps casual onlookers out of a flash zone. It is a starting box, not a verdict. The ERG initial isolation distance assumes you have identified the product and read the weather right. If you can't name the material, the table can't help you yet, so you default conservative. A leaking drum on a loading dock and a placarded tanker venting toward a school are not the same problem, and the same 50 meters that's generous for one is reckless for the other.

items.title: Wind pushes it
items.body: Vapor and gas travel downwind. Set your hot zone larger on the downwind side and stage your apparatus upwind and uphill, never below the release.

items.title: Slope pulls it
items.body: Heavier-than-air gases and liquid runoff flow downhill into culverts, basements, and storm drains. Walk the low ground before you trust it.

items.title: Crowds breach it
items.body: Phones, traffic, and curiosity drag bystanders toward the scene. The perimeter only exists where someone is physically holding the line.

blocks.title: What drives an isolation distance outward (illustrative)
blocks.note: Illustrative weighting of factors that commonly force responders to expand a perimeter — not measured incident data.

blocks.text: The distance that feels too big from the cab is the distance you'll wish you had from the burn unit.
blocks.attribution: Hazmat team leader, metro fire department

blocks.title: Expand the perimeter now — don't wait to confirm
items: You can see vapor, mist, or a visible cloud drifting from the source.
Anyone reports or shows symptoms: coughing, burning eyes, dizziness, skin irritation, difficulty breathing.
The container is bulging, hissing, venting, or radiating heat you can feel from a distance.
The product is still unidentified 5 minutes after arrival — default to Tier 2 isolation (>150 m) and request hazmat-1.
The wind shifts toward populated areas, a school, or a highway — move the line, don't debate it.

blocks.title: Identify the clock, not just the chemical
blocks.body: Start a mental timer on arrival. Use placards, container shape, shipping papers, and the ERG to name the product fast. If you have it, the orange-bordered guide pages and the green-bordered isolation tables give you a defensible distance. If you don't have it inside five minutes, stop hunting and default up: Tier 2 isolation beyond 150 meters and a hazmat-1 request to the dispatcher. An unidentified product is a worst-case product until proven otherwise. The most common mistake is treating the wait for ID as neutral time — it isn't. People are accumulating dose while you read.

blocks.title: Where responders get it wrong
blocks.body: Two failures repeat. First, anchoring on the first number: crews set 50 meters, get comfortable, and never revisit it when the wind turns or a second victim appears. Second, contracting too early — pulling the line back on a hunch instead of on a meter reading. Isolation only shrinks when air monitoring confirms it, in writing, from a calibrated instrument. Until then, every change is one direction: outward. Park upwind and uphill, keep your escape route open, and never let your own apparatus end up inside the zone you just drew.

items.body: Approach from upwind and uphill, stop short, and position apparatus for a clean exit.
Set an initial isolation of at least 50 m, larger downwind and downslope, and assign someone to hold each side.
Work placards, container shape, papers, and the ERG to name the product and pull its distance.
No ID in 5 minutes — go Tier 2 (>150 m) and request hazmat-1. Re-expand on any vapor, heat, or symptom.
Only contract the perimeter after air monitoring confirms the atmosphere is safe.

blocks.title: On arrival, in order
The takeaway
blocks.body: Initial isolation distance is a decision you keep making, not one you make once. Set it big, keep it honest against wind, slope, and symptoms, and let it shrink only when the air tells you it's safe. The responders who go home are the ones who treated the perimeter as living — willing to move people back one more time, even when it felt like overkill. Recognize, isolate, notify. Isolation is the step that buys time for the other two.

blocks.title: Cleanly handing the IC role
The call that sets everything in motion
blocks.body: You've recognized the hazard and isolated the area. Now you have to put it into someone else's head over a radio that crackles, in a window of maybe fifteen seconds. The notification you give next decides how fast the right resources roll, where they stage, and whether the next unit drives into the cloud or stops upwind of it. A precise sitrep beats a long one. Lead with location, product, isolation, and resources requested — then stop talking and let dispatch work.

blocks.title: Why precision wins over volume
blocks.body: Under stress your instinct is to narrate everything you see. Resist it. Dispatch and the incoming hazmat team need decisions, not a story. A bloated transmission buries the one fact that matters — the placard number, the wind direction, the size of your hot zone — under detail nobody can act on yet. Tight, ordered information also forces you to confirm what you actually know versus what you're guessing. If you can't read the placard, say 'placard not yet identified' rather than inventing a product. Honest gaps are safer than confident errors.

items.title: Location
items.body: Exact address or cross streets, your position relative to the release, and which side is upwind. Give the incoming units a safe approach, not just a destination.

items.title: Product & isolation
items.body: Placard ID number, NFPA 704 readout, or 'unknown.' State your isolation distance and whether the public is being moved or sheltered.

items.title: Resources requested
items.body: Hazmat team, additional engines, EMS, law for traffic, the CHEMTREC or ERG reference you're working from. Name what you need now.

blocks.title: Where the first sitrep's words should go
blocks.note: Illustrative weighting of an effective initial transmission — not a fixed rule. The point is balance: no single element should crowd out the others.

blocks.text: Tell me where it is, what it is, how far you've pushed people back, and what you need. Everything else can wait for the next radio traffic.

blocks.title: Red flags that change your notification
items: Placard or NFPA readout you can't identify from a safe distance — report it as unknown, do not guess the product.
Wind shift that puts your staging area or the public downwind — re-transmit isolation immediately.
Visible vapor cloud, pooling liquid, or pressure-relief venting — escalate resources before you're asked.
Multiple patients showing the same symptoms — suspect the release is larger than it looks and call for more EMS.
Any sign the incident crosses your agency's capability — request mutual aid early; it is faster to cancel than to wait.

blocks.title: The handoff to Command
blocks.body: Your first transmission buys time; the handoff to the arriving Incident Commander or hazmat team makes it count. When they reach you, give a face-to-face briefing in the same order you radioed: what you have, what you've done, and what's still open. Then formally transfer command — say it out loud, 'You have command,' and confirm they accept. The most common failure here is the silent handoff, where the first-arriving officer drifts back into the scene without ever clearing who is running it. Two people thinking they're in charge is the same as nobody being in charge.

blocks.title: Speak the system, not just the scene
blocks.body: Once ICS is established, fold your language into it. You are no longer 'the first guy here' — you're a resource with an assignment, reporting to a position. Use the agreed staging area, keep your radio traffic on the assigned channel, and route requests through the chain rather than freelancing on the air. The structure exists so that a chaotic scene scales cleanly as more units arrive. Your discipline on the radio is what lets it.

items.body: Give address or cross streets, your position, and the upwind safe approach for incoming units.
Report the placard number, NFPA 704 readout, or state clearly that the product is unknown.
State your isolation distance and whether the public is being evacuated or sheltered in place.
Name the specific resources you need — hazmat, EMS, mutual aid — and any reference source you're using.
Brief Command in the same order, transfer command verbally, and confirm it was accepted.

blocks.title: Run the notification in this order
The takeaway
blocks.body: Notification is not paperwork you do after the work — it is the work. Four ordered facts and a clean command transfer turn one set of eyes into a coordinated response. Lead with location, product, isolation, and resources, hand off out loud, and let the system carry the weight. Say less, say it in order, and the right help arrives ready.

courses.title: Critical Thinking — Foundations
courses.summary: Recognize claims, separate evidence from assertion, and structure a defensible argument.
courses.credibility: Reviewed by your faculty advisor; aligned to the campus rhetoric standard.

blocks.title: What an argument actually is
The skeleton under every argument
blocks.body: When a student writes "social media harms teenagers" and pastes in three statistics, they think they've made an argument. They haven't. They've made an assertion and dropped some numbers near it. Every real argument has three load-bearing parts, and once you can name them, you can see exactly where any argument holds and where it collapses. This is the first move in critical thinking: take the thing apart before you judge it.

blocks.title: Claim, evidence, warrant
blocks.body: The claim is what you want the reader to accept — the conclusion. The evidence is the observable, checkable support: a study, a dataset, a quotation, a test result. The warrant is the reasoning that connects the two — the unstated "because this evidence, therefore this claim." Claim: students who sleep more score higher. Evidence: a survey linking sleep hours to GPA. Warrant: that correlation reflects sleep causing performance, not the reverse and not a hidden third factor. Notice the warrant is where the real work happens — and where it's almost always left silent.

items.title: Claim
items.body: The assertion you're asking someone to accept. State it as one sentence — if you can't, you have more than one claim tangled together.

items.title: Evidence
items.body: What you can point to and verify: data, sources, observations. Evidence is shared ground; two people should be able to check it independently.

items.title: Warrant
items.body: The bridge. Why this evidence supports this claim. Usually unspoken — which is exactly why weak arguments hide here.

blocks.title: Where student arguments break down (writing-center review)
blocks.note: Illustrative distribution based on a composite of writing-center tutoring patterns — not a single published dataset.

blocks.text: Students don't lose points for weak evidence nearly as often as for never explaining why the evidence matters.

blocks.title: Red flags: the warrant is missing or broken
items: A statistic is presented and the argument moves on as if the conclusion is now obvious.
The evidence measures one thing but the claim is about another (test scores cited to prove "learning").
"Studies show" with no account of what the study actually found or how it connects.
Correlation is treated as cause with no reasoning offered for the direction.
The claim is so broad that no single piece of evidence could ever reach it.

blocks.title: Why the warrant goes missing
blocks.body: Warrants disappear because they feel obvious to the person making the argument. You already believe the connection, so you don't notice you skipped stating it. That's also why warrants are where bias hides: an unstated assumption never gets examined. The discipline is to drag the warrant into the open and ask, "Would a fair-minded skeptic grant this step?" If the evidence is a single classroom's results and the claim is about all learners, the warrant — "this classroom represents everyone" — is doing enormous work it can't support.

blocks.title: Stress-test the bridge, not just the ends
blocks.body: Most people, asked to critique an argument, attack the claim ("I disagree") or nitpick the evidence ("that's an old study"). The sharper move is to attack the warrant. Grant the evidence as true for a moment, then ask: does it actually get you to the claim? Often the evidence is solid and the leap is the problem. A reading-time study might be airtight and still not prove that assigning more reading raises comprehension — the warrant connecting "time spent" to "caused improvement" is the weak plank.

items.body: State the single conclusion in one sentence. If it won't fit, separate the claims and handle each on its own.
Name exactly what is offered as support and confirm it's checkable, not just another assertion.
Write the unstated "because… therefore…" out loud. This is the step almost everyone skips.
Grant the evidence, then ask whether the reasoning really reaches the claim. Look for the hidden assumption.
Decide whether the claim, the evidence, or the warrant is doing work it can't support — then aim your critique there.

blocks.title: How to dissect any argument
The takeaway
blocks.body: An argument isn't strong because it has data — it's strong because the data, the conclusion, and the reasoning between them all hold under pressure. From here on, never accept evidence at face value or reject a claim on instinct. Find all three parts, say the warrant out loud, and test the bridge. Do that and you've stopped reacting to arguments and started reading them. That habit is the foundation everything else in this course is built on.

courses.title: Lockout / Tagout — Refresher
courses.summary: Six-step LOTO sequence, energy-isolation verification, and exception handling for shift transitions.
courses.credibility: OSHA 1910.147-aligned; reviewed by site EHS lead.

blocks.title: Notify, shut down, isolate, lock, dissipate, verify
Locked is not the same as safe
blocks.body: LOTO runs as six steps, in order, every time: notify, shut down, isolate, lock, dissipate, verify. The order is not a suggestion — each step disarms a different hazard, and the sequence ends with verify for a reason. A locked disconnect tells you the supply path is broken. It tells you nothing about the energy still trapped downstream: a charged capacitor bank, a raised hydraulic ram, a spring under tension, steam in a header. Verify is where you stop trusting the diagram and start trusting a meter, a gauge, and your own hands on the controls.

blocks.title: Why verify is the step people drop
blocks.body: The first five steps feel like progress — you walk the floor, hit the stop, throw the disconnect, snap on your padlock and tag. By then the equipment looks dead, and the temptation is to climb in. That confidence is exactly the trap. Stored energy doesn't care that the breaker is off. A conveyor gearbox can roll backward under load, an accumulator can drive a cylinder with the pump dead, and a 480V drive can hold a lethal charge for minutes after isolation. Verify is the only step that proves the system reached a zero-energy state instead of assuming it.

items.title: Isolate breaks the path
items.body: Opening the disconnect or valve cuts the supply. It does not drain what's already past that point in the system.

items.title: Lock holds the state
items.body: Your padlock and personal tag keep the isolation point from being re-energized. One lock per worker, no shared keys.

items.title: Verify proves zero
items.body: Test the meter, bleed the line, try the start button. Confirm dead before any body part enters the danger zone.

blocks.title: Where stored-energy incidents trace back
blocks.note: Illustrative breakdown for training discussion — not a published incident dataset.

blocks.text: I've never been hurt by a machine I knew was dead. I've been scared by the ones I assumed were.

blocks.title: Stop and re-verify when you see any of these
items: A pressure gauge that hasn't dropped to zero, or a hydraulic line that still feels firm
Drives, VFDs, or capacitor cabinets that were energized in the last few minutes
Suspended loads, raised platforms, or counterweights still under gravity
A start button that gets any response at all when you test for dead
You returned from break or a shift change and didn't witness the lockout yourself

blocks.title: What verify actually looks like on the floor
blocks.body: Verify is an active test, not a glance. For electrical work, you test your meter on a known live source, test the isolated conductors, then test the meter again to prove it still reads. For stored energy, you dissipate first — bleed hydraulic and pneumatic pressure to zero, drain or block accumulators, discharge capacitors, release spring tension, chock or lower suspended parts — then confirm at the gauge. Finally you attempt to start: press the controls and confirm nothing moves. Only when all three checks read dead does the equipment become work-ready.

blocks.title: The shift-transition gap
blocks.body: Most refresher failures aren't on the original lockout — they're at handoff. The day-shift tech isolates and verifies, then leaves. Night shift sees locks and tags hanging and assumes the work was verified for them. It wasn't. A lockout you didn't witness is a lockout you re-verify. If the job carries across a shift change, the incoming worker applies their own lock and runs their own try-test before trusting the zero-energy state.

items.body: Tell every affected operator and supervisor before the equipment goes down.
Stop the equipment normally, then open the disconnect or valve at the correct isolation point.
Apply your own padlock and personal tag. One lock per worker, key in your pocket.
Drain, bleed, discharge, block, or release every form of stored energy until gauges read zero.
Test the meter live-dead-live, confirm gauges, then press start and confirm nothing moves.

blocks.title: Run the sequence — every step, every time
The step that ends the sequence
blocks.body: Five steps make the equipment look safe. The sixth step proves it. Verify is the difference between trusting a procedure and confirming a result — and it's the one step that stands between you and the energy you can't see. Lock it, dissipate it, then prove it's dead before you reach in. Every time, no exceptions, even when you're sure.

courses.title: Sepsis Bundle — May Update
courses.summary: Recognize early sepsis, initiate the bundle within the hour, and document defensibly.
courses.credibility: Aligned to SSC 2024 guidance; reviewed by ED and ICU leads.

blocks.title: qSOFA in triage
A flag, not a finding
blocks.body: qSOFA isn't a diagnosis. It's a tripwire. When a patient scores two of three — respiratory rate 22 or higher, altered mentation, systolic BP 100 or lower — it doesn't mean they're septic, and it doesn't mean you launch the bundle on autopilot. It means the floor under your assessment just dropped. Re-eval now, not at the next vitals cycle. The whole point of catching sepsis early is that the window is narrow and it closes quietly.

blocks.title: Why bedside speed matters
blocks.body: qSOFA was built to be fast and tool-free — no labs, no calculator, just three things you can read off a patient in fifteen seconds. That's the design intent: surface high-risk patients outside the ICU before the lactate comes back, before the pressure tanks. A positive score is a prompt to escalate your suspicion and your scrutiny, pull a lactate, look harder for a source, and loop in the provider. A negative score is not a clearance — a patient with one criterion and a wrong gut feeling still gets your attention.

items.title: RR ≥ 22
items.body: The earliest and most-missed criterion. Tachypnea precedes hypotension by hours. Count a full 30 seconds — don't trust the monitor's number.

items.title: Altered mentation
items.body: Any drop from baseline — GCS < 15, new confusion, 'just not themselves.' Family noticing a change counts. Subtle beats absent.

items.title: SBP ≤ 100
items.body: A late and ominous sign. By the time pressure falls, compensation is failing. Don't wait for this one to take the other two seriously.

blocks.title: Which qSOFA criterion shows up first
blocks.note: Illustrative distribution of the first qSOFA criterion to turn positive in ward patients who later met sepsis criteria. Tachypnea leads — which is exactly why a quiet respiratory rate gets overlooked.

blocks.text: The patient who's breathing fast and sounds a little off is the one I worry about — not the one whose pressure already crashed. By then I'm playing catch-up.

blocks.title: Re-evaluate now — don't wait for the next cycle
items: Two qSOFA criteria in a patient with a plausible infection source (urinary, pulmonary, skin, line, abdominal)
A rising respiratory rate trending up over the last few hours, even if still under 22
New confusion or somnolence that family or staff flag as off-baseline
A single criterion plus a worsening trajectory — your suspicion outweighs a borderline number
Any qSOFA-positive patient who hasn't had a lactate drawn

blocks.title: The trap: treating the score as the decision
blocks.body: The most common mistake isn't missing the criteria — it's mistaking what they mean. qSOFA was never built to capture every septic patient; it favors specificity over sensitivity, so it will miss early sepsis that hasn't tipped the bedside yet. Treating a negative score as reassurance is how a patient with a UTI and a fever of 38.9 sits another two hours. Run it the other direction: a positive score escalates your concern, a negative score never overrides it. The score informs the clinician. It doesn't replace one.

blocks.title: What 'raising the bar for re-eval' actually means
blocks.body: Re-eval isn't repeating vitals. It's a full second look: source of infection, lactate, mental status against baseline, urine output, skin and capillary refill, and the trajectory across the last several readings. You're deciding whether this is a stable patient with one odd number or a patient sliding toward organ dysfunction. That judgment — not the qSOFA tally — is what triggers the provider call and starts the clock on the hour-1 bundle. The flag gets you to the bedside; your assessment decides what happens next.

items.body: Recount the respiratory rate over a full 30 seconds and reassess mentation against the patient's documented baseline — not the monitor's snapshot.
Scan for a plausible infection: urinary, pulmonary, skin or wound, line, or abdominal. A flag with a source is a different animal than a flag without one.
Get the lactate moving and a full vitals set. This is data the score can't give you and the bundle will demand.
Call it as a re-eval, not a maybe. Communicate the criteria met, the suspected source, and the trajectory.
Note what flagged, when you reassessed, and what you escalated — this is where defensible documentation starts.

blocks.title: When qSOFA flags, do this in order
The takeaway
blocks.body: qSOFA earns its keep by being fast and easy to miss the meaning of. Two of three raises the bar for re-evaluation — it sends you to the bedside with sharper eyes and a lactate order, not into an automatic protocol. Catch the tachypnea early, trust your read of the patient over a borderline number, and let your assessment, not the score, decide when the hour-1 clock starts.

courses.title: Patient Assessment on a Routine Call
courses.summary: Run a single-patient medical call cleanly — scene safety, vitals, communication.
courses.credibility: Aligned to NREMT assessment objectives; reviewed by your training officer.

blocks.title: First 30 seconds on a medical call
The first thirty seconds belong to you
blocks.body: Before you ever touch the patient, the call has already started. You're rolling up, door not yet open, and your job is to read the scene before you commit your body to it. Hazards, mechanism, number of patients, and where your team fits — that's the size-up. It happens fast, it happens out loud, and it's the difference between one patient and three. The work here is observation, not action. In that first half-minute your only two goals are to not get hurt and to set the tone for everything that follows.

blocks.title: Read the scene, not just the patient
blocks.body: Tunnel vision is the enemy. A patient down on the floor pulls your eyes like a magnet, and that's exactly when you miss the frayed extension cord, the dog in the back room, the spouse pacing with clenched fists, the faint smell of gas. Start wide and work in: the block, the address, the doorway, the room, then the patient. Scene size-up is a deliberate habit of looking up and around when every instinct says look down. The patient will still be there in five seconds. The hazard that drops you won't wait.

items.title: Hazards
items.body: Traffic, downed lines, fire, fluids, animals, weapons, agitated bystanders. If it can hurt you, name it before you step in.

items.title: Mechanism / nature
items.body: MOI for trauma, NOI for medical. What did this to them tells you what to look for and how bad it may get.

items.title: Numbers & resources
items.body: How many patients? Do you have the hands and the rig for it? If not, call for more before you're committed.

blocks.title: Where responder injuries on scene come from
blocks.note: Illustrative distribution to show why the size-up looks outward first — exact figures vary by agency and call type.

blocks.text: If the scene isn't safe, you don't have a patient — you have two.

blocks.title: Stop and reassess — red flags that mean don't enter
items: Anything that reads as a violent or unstable scene — wait for law enforcement to clear it.
Visible weapons, or a patient or bystander who is escalating toward you.
Unknown spills, vapors, placards, or a strange smell — stage upwind and uphill.
Traffic still moving or no upstream blocking — your rig and cones go first.
More patients than you can manage — call it as an MCI and request resources now.

blocks.title: Say it out loud
blocks.body: Size-up isn't a private thought — it's a callout. "Scene safe, one patient, no hazards, BSI on" tells your partner where your head is and assigns lanes without a meeting. The same voice does double duty: a calm, even tone broadcast to the patient and the room sets the emotional thermostat for the whole call. People take their cues from how you walk in. Rushed and frantic spreads; deliberate and steady settles a room. You are managing the scene's nervous system before you ever take a pulse.

blocks.title: The common mistakes
blocks.body: New responders skip the size-up because the patient looks urgent — and that urgency is precisely the bait. The other failure is treating size-up as a one-time gate at the door. Scenes change: a quiet living room fills with arriving family, a stable patient's blood sugar bottoms out, a leak you didn't smell at first builds. Size-up is continuous. Glance up between vitals. If the scene shifts, your size-up resets, and you are allowed to retreat. Backing out of a scene that turned is not a failure — it's the system working.

items.body: Don BSI/PPE before contact. Park to protect, set blocking and cones, scan for the obvious struck-by and struck-down risks.
Eyes wide before narrow — hazards, exits, animals, and people. If it isn't safe, stage and wait; don't enter to fix it.
Trauma: what hit what, how hard. Medical: what's the complaint and the surroundings telling you.
Confirm patient number and request additional resources before you're committed to a single patient.
Call "scene safe" with the headline, assign lanes, then approach the patient calm and deliberate.

blocks.title: Run the size-up in order
The takeaway
blocks.body: Scene size-up is the cheapest, highest-leverage thirty seconds of the entire call. You haven't laid a hand on anyone yet, but you've already decided whether this stays a one-patient routine call or becomes something worse. Look up before you look down, say what you see, and keep looking the whole time you're there. Stay safe, set the tone — then go to work.

blocks.title: ABC, vitals, and the focused history
Find the killers first
blocks.body: On a routine medical call, the patient who looks fine can still be the one in trouble. The primary survey is how you catch life threats in the first sixty seconds, before you ever pull a blood pressure cuff. You run airway, breathing, circulation in that order — A, B, C — because that's the order they kill. A blocked airway drops a patient faster than a low pressure ever will. Work the sequence the same way every time so that under stress your hands know the order even when your head is racing.

blocks.title: A before B before C
blocks.body: Airway: is it open, is it staying open, is anything threatening it — blood, vomit, swelling, a slumped tongue? Breathing: look at chest rise, count the rate, listen to lung sounds, feel for work of breathing and accessory muscle use. Circulation: check a radial pulse, scan skin color, temperature and moisture, and find any obvious bleeding and stop it. Each step gates the next. You don't move to breathing while the airway is compromised, and you don't chase a vitals number while someone is bleeding out in front of you. Fix what you find before you advance.

items.title: Rate
items.body: How fast. A respiratory rate of 28 or a pulse of 130 reframes everything you see next — speed is your earliest warning.

items.title: Quality
items.body: How strong. A thready, weak radial pulse or shallow, labored breaths tell you the body is working too hard to compensate.

items.title: Rhythm
items.body: How regular. An irregular pulse or irregular breathing pattern points at the underlying problem a single number hides.

blocks.title: Why three beats one
blocks.body: A single number lies easily. A pulse of 90 reads normal on paper — but if it's weak and irregular, that 90 is a patient compensating, not a patient who's fine. Rate, quality, and rhythm together do more diagnostic work than any one figure on your run sheet. Train yourself to capture all three on every pulse and every set of respirations. The trend across two sets, taken minutes apart, tells you more than any single snapshot: a rate climbing call to call is the story, not the first number you wrote down.

blocks.title: Where field crews catch deterioration first
blocks.note: Illustrative distribution of the first sign crews report noticing on calls that later turned critical — directional, not from a specific dataset.

blocks.text: The monitor tells you what the number is. Your hands on a radial pulse tell you what it means.

blocks.title: Red flags — interrupt the survey and act
items: Airway you can't keep open — stridor, gurgling, or a patient who can't speak in full sentences.
Respiratory rate under 8 or over 30, or rising sharply between your two sets.
Radial pulse you can barely feel, or one that's fast and irregular together.
Skin that's pale, cool, and clammy — early shock often shows on the skin before the pressure drops.
Any patient whose mental status is dropping as you work — that overrides every vital on the sheet.

blocks.title: Where it goes wrong
blocks.body: The common mistakes are predictable. Crews skip straight to the BP cuff because it feels like 'doing something,' and miss the labored breathing in front of them. They write a rate down as 'normal' without actually counting for a full fifteen seconds. They take one set of vitals and never repeat it, so they never see the trend. And they let a talkative, walking patient talk them out of a real survey. Slow is smooth, smooth is fast — count what you can count, and don't let a calm scene make you sloppy.

items.body: Confirm it's open and staying open. Clear or position before you do anything else.
Count the rate for a full fifteen seconds, note quality and effort, listen to lung sounds.
Find a radial pulse — rate, quality, rhythm — check skin, and control any visible bleeding.
Capture BP, pulse-ox, and your A-B-C findings as a baseline, and note the time.
Take a second set a few minutes later. The trend between the two is your real picture.

blocks.title: Run it in this order, every call
The takeaway
blocks.body: A clean primary survey isn't about speed for its own sake — it's about catching the life threat before it catches your patient. Run A-B-C in the same order every time, capture rate, quality, and rhythm on every pulse and every set of breaths, and take a second set so you can see which way the patient is heading. Do that consistently and you'll spot the patient who's quietly deteriorating long before a single number on the monitor ever sounds the alarm.

blocks.prompt: A conscious adult patient with chest pain is breathing 18, pulse 88 strong and regular, BP 132/84. Your next move?

options.label: Start a focused history (OPQRST) while continuing to monitor
options.feedback: Right — they're stable. The chest pain history is what shapes treatment from here.

options.label: Apply oxygen immediately at 15L/min
options.feedback: No clinical indication. Routine high-flow O2 in a stable patient can do harm.

options.label: Move directly to transport without further assessment
options.feedback: You'd be transporting without the information that shapes destination and report.

blocks.title: The fast reload
blocks.body: You've already shown this instinct in the field. Your last scenario proved you read scene safety before you read the patient, which is exactly the move that keeps a compounding call from collapsing on you. So treat this as a refresher, not a rebuild. A compounding scene is one where the original problem keeps spawning new ones: the MVC that becomes a fuel leak that becomes a crowd-control problem that becomes a second patient nobody flagged. The skill isn't reacting fast. It's keeping a wide enough frame that the next hazard doesn't surprise you. Reload the frame, then move on if it already lives in your hands.

blocks.title: Why scenes compound
blocks.body: Most bad outcomes on complex calls don't come from the first hazard. They come from tunnel vision on it. You commit to the patient on the pavement and stop scanning, so you miss the downed line arcing six feet behind you, the bystander stepping into traffic, or the agitated family member closing distance at your back. Compounding scenes punish fixation. The discipline is to scan in layers — environment, then threats, then patients, then access and egress — and to re-scan on a clock, because a scene that was safe on arrival is a different scene ninety seconds later.

items.title: Static hazards
items.body: Fixed and visible on arrival: traffic, terrain, downed lines, leaking fuel, structural instability. You can usually stage around these.

items.title: Dynamic hazards
items.body: They move and change: fire spread, agitated bystanders, crowds, weather, an animal. These need a re-scan clock, not a single glance.

items.title: Hidden hazards
items.body: Not obvious from the curb: a second patient, a weapon, gas, an unstable vehicle. Assume they exist until your size-up rules them out.

blocks.title: Where size-up time tends to go on a compounding scene
blocks.note: Illustrative only — proportions shift by call type, but the point holds: more than half your early attention is the scene, not the patient.

blocks.text: The scene that hurts you is the one you stopped looking at. Eyes up, head on a swivel, until somebody relieves you of it.
blocks.attribution: Veteran field training officer, fire-based EMS

blocks.title: Stop and re-stage when you see these
items: A hazard you can't control with what's on scene — fuel, fire, electrical, structural
Patient count climbing past your crew's capacity to manage at once
Bystanders or family closing distance, or any indication of a weapon
Your only exit route is now blocked by traffic, crowd, or apparatus
A scent, sound, or symptom pattern that suggests gas, CO, or hazmat

blocks.title: The common miss
blocks.body: The mistake isn't failing to spot the first hazard — it's failing to update. You did a clean size-up, called it safe, and then mentally filed the scene as 'handled' while you worked the patient. Compounding scenes don't stay filed. The fix is cheap: assign the re-scan. On a two-person crew, one of you owns the patient and one owns the scene, and you trade verbal updates. On a bigger response, that's literally what the safety officer is for. If nobody owns the scene, everybody assumes someone else does, and that gap is where the second hazard walks in.

blocks.title: Naming it out loud
blocks.body: Say what you see. 'I've got a second patient in the ditch,' 'fuel's pooling toward us,' 'crowd's growing on my left' — short, declarative, directed. Naming a hazard does three things at once: it moves the threat from your head into the crew's shared picture, it forces you to decide whether it changes the plan, and it gives dispatch and incoming units a reason to adjust resources before they arrive. Silent recognition helps no one. The hazard you noticed but didn't announce is functionally a hazard nobody caught.

items.body: Terrain, traffic, structure, weather, access and egress — before you touch anyone.
People, animals, weapons, violence indicators. Position so you're never boxed in.
Confirm the number before you commit to one. A second patient changes everything downstream.
Call backup early, while it's cheap. Canceling is easy; waiting is not.
Assign who owns the scene and keep updating out loud until transport or relief.

blocks.title: Run the frame in order
The takeaway
blocks.body: You already lead with scene safety — that's the win, and it's why you can move quickly through this. The one upgrade a compounding scene asks for is rhythm: don't size up once, size up continuously, and make sure someone owns that re-scan while someone else owns the patient. Keep the frame wide, name what changes, and the second hazard stops being a surprise. If that's already automatic for you, skip ahead. If you want it sharper, run a call in your head right now and ask: who had eyes up the whole time?

blocks.title: When the picture is changing faster than you can read it
The field gets smaller, not bigger
blocks.body: When a call goes sideways — a multi-vehicle wreck with entrapment, a structure fire with a reported occupant, a scene that turns violent on arrival — your instinct is to gather more. More radio traffic, more visual sweep, more confirmation. Under load, that instinct works against you. The job in those first seconds is to narrow the field, not widen it. Pick the next-best action you can defend in ten seconds, commit to it, and re-read the scene. Indecision burns more time than an imperfect choice, and on a working call, time is the resource you can never recover.

blocks.title: Why your brain narrows on you
blocks.body: Stress is not a character flaw to push through; it is physiology. As load climbs, your heart rate spikes, fine motor skills degrade, hearing narrows, and your working memory shrinks to a handful of items. You literally hold fewer options in your head than you do at the kitchen table. Fighting this by trying to consider everything is how responders freeze on scene. The skilled move is to work *with* the narrowing: pre-load a small set of defensible actions before you arrive, then choose from that short list instead of building one from scratch while your tank is redlining.

items.title: Narrow the inputs
items.body: Triage what you read. Life threat, scene safety, then everything else. Ignore the noise that does not change your next action.

items.title: Commit the output
items.body: Make one decision and act on it fully. A half-committed action on a working call is usually worse than the wrong one done cleanly.

items.title: Re-read the loop
items.body: Decisions are not final. Act, observe what changed, decide again. The scene votes on whether you were right.

blocks.title: The ten-second defense test
blocks.body: Before you commit, run a fast gut check: could you justify this action to your captain in ten seconds, using what you can see right now? If yes, move. "I established a water supply before attacking because the hydrant was the only one within reach" passes. "I wasn't sure, so I waited" does not. The test is not about being right in hindsight — it is about being defensible in the moment with the information you actually had. That standard keeps you decisive without making you reckless.

data.label: Waiting for someone else to call it
Weighing options past the point of value

blocks.title: Where seconds go on a stalled decision
blocks.note: Illustrative breakdown of time spent during a hesitation on scene — the actual action is the smallest slice.

blocks.text: A good decision now beats a perfect one too late. The scene won't wait for your certainty.
blocks.attribution: Fire department battalion chief, 22 years on the line

blocks.title: Red flags that you've stalled out
items: You're asking for the same information a second or third time over the radio.
Your crew is standing by, looking at you, waiting for a task.
You're narrating the problem instead of assigning an action.
You catch yourself waiting for the situation to 'become clear' before you move.
The clock has moved but nothing on scene has changed because of you.

blocks.title: The common trap: optimizing under fire
blocks.body: The most frequent failure isn't panic — it's quiet over-analysis. You try to find the best option when a good-enough one is sitting in front of you. Experienced responders don't compare every possibility; they recognize a pattern, match it to an action that has worked before, and run it. This is recognition-primed decision-making, and it's why veterans look calm: they're not choosing from twenty options, they're confirming one. You build that library through reps, not by thinking harder in the moment.

blocks.title: Decisive is not the same as fast
blocks.body: Narrowing the field does not mean rushing. A deliberate pause to size up — circling the structure, reading mechanism of injury, confirming the scene is safe to enter — is itself a committed action, not indecision. The difference is intent. Stalling is waiting for the call to make itself. Sizing up is gathering the one or two facts that change your next move, then moving. If the information you're waiting for wouldn't alter what you do next, you don't need it.

items.body: Scan for life threat and scene safety first. Stop gathering once you have enough to pick a defensible next action.
Two or three options, drawn from training and prior calls — not an open-ended search.
Pick the action you could justify out loud right now, then commit to it fully.
Give your crew a clear task. A committed imperfect action beats a perfect intention.
Observe what changed, then run the loop again. Stay in the cycle until the call is stable.

blocks.title: Run this loop under load
The takeaway
blocks.body: Under load, your edge isn't knowing more — it's deciding cleaner. Narrow the field, choose the action you can defend in ten seconds, commit, and re-read. Do that on every call, and your decisions get faster and your scenes get safer, not because the calls got easier, but because you stopped waiting for certainty that was never coming.

concepts.label: Recognizing high-risk drinking and impairment cues

blocks.title: What high-risk drinking actually looks like

flow.title: Reading the scene
flow.intro: Take note of what you see in each scene. After reviewing the last scene, we'll talk through what you observed.

scenes.title: Scene 1 — The party
scenes.description: It's late and the party is still going. Most of the night has looked completely ordinary — until it doesn't. Watch how a normal evening tips toward a moment that needs someone to act.

scenes.title: Scene 2 — Sam's signs
scenes.description: Impairment shows up first in speech, balance, and judgment — not in falling down. Sam is slurring, unsteady, and arguing with someone they barely know.

scenes.title: Scene 3 — Final actions
scenes.description: Sam is now reaching for the car keys and heading for the door. The same cues carry very different risk depending on what comes next — and nobody else seems to be tracking it.

blocks.title: Procedural overview
blocks.body: Before you can intervene, you have to notice. This lesson covers the impairment cues that matter most at a party — speech, balance, judgment under pressure — and how they shift the risk picture when a car, a stairwell, or a stranger enters the scene. By the end you'll have a quick read you can run in seconds, almost without thinking.

blocks.alt: A crowded house party at night
blocks.caption: Most high-risk moments don't look dramatic. They look like an ordinary party — until one person stops tracking what's happening around them.

blocks.title: Impairment is a spectrum, not a switch
blocks.body: Nobody goes from "fine" to "emergency" in one step. Alcohol affects the brain from the top down — judgment and self-awareness fade first, then coordination, then the basics that keep someone safe. That's why the person in trouble often doesn't feel like they're in trouble: the part of the brain that would notice is the first part offline.

items.title: Speech & language
items.body: Slurred, slowed, or repetitive. Losing the thread of a conversation or answering a different question than the one asked.

items.title: Balance & motor
items.body: Swaying, reaching for walls, fumbling a phone or a cup. Stairs and curbs become genuinely risky.

items.title: Judgment & attention
items.body: Decisions that don't fit the moment — wandering off alone, trusting a stranger, insisting on driving.

blocks.title: The cues that matter most
blocks.body: Impairment shows up first in fine motor control and judgment, not in falling down. You're not diagnosing anyone — you're noticing a change from how this person usually is. A friend who's normally sharp going quiet and unsteady is a bigger signal than a stranger who's loud.

blocks.title: Signs students notice first
blocks.note: Cues college students say they'd flag in a friend. Illustrative campus-survey data.

blocks.text: The loudest person at the party is rarely the one in trouble. The quiet one slumped in the corner usually is.

blocks.title: Read the cue and the context together
blocks.body: The same cues carry very different risk depending on what comes next. "A little drunk" on a couch is not the same as "a little drunk" at the top of a staircase, behind a wheel, or walking home alone. A cue you'd shrug off in a safe room becomes the whole story the moment the scene changes — so read the person and the situation at the same time.

blocks.alt: A hand holding out a set of car keys in front of a car
blocks.caption: "Getting home safe" is the cue that most often gets overridden — taking the keys is a small act with an outsized effect.

blocks.title: Stop watching and step in when you see
items: They can't be woken, or only briefly
Slow, irregular, or noisy breathing
Cold, clammy, or bluish skin; repeated vomiting
They're about to drive, or get in a stranger's car
They're heading off alone — stairs, water, or out into the cold

blocks.title: What good bystanders actually do
blocks.body: Stepping in almost never means a dramatic rescue. It's small, early, and quiet: a glass of water, sitting down next to someone, walking them to a friend, or quietly flagging an RA. The students who act aren't braver than everyone else — they just trusted the feeling that something was off instead of waiting for someone else to move first.

blocks.alt: Four friends with their arms around each other at sunset
blocks.caption: The people most likely to step in are friends who already sensed something felt off — and trusted that read.

blocks.title: What students did when a friend was in trouble
blocks.note: More than one action could be selected. The gap between noticing and acting is where this course focuses.

blocks.title: Your quick read, in order

items.body: Who here looks different from how they were an hour ago?
Speech, balance, judgment — how many, and how strong?
What's about to happen — stairs, a car, leaving alone?
Water, stay close, a ride, or a word to someone who can help.

blocks.title: Your job tonight
blocks.body: You don't need to be a medic. You need to notice early, stay close, and make one good call — a glass of water, a stay-with-them, a ride, or a word to someone who can help. The next lessons turn each of those into something you can actually say and do.

blocks.title: The gap between seeing and doing
blocks.body: You will almost certainly be the one in the room when something goes wrong — at the dorm pre-game, the off-campus house party, the tailgate. Research on campus drinking is blunt about this: students witness far more high-risk situations than staff or RAs ever do. The problem is rarely that nobody noticed. It is that everyone noticed and assumed someone else would handle it. This lesson closes that gap. You will learn the five-step frame that turns a witness into an ally, and the low-friction scripts that let you step in without making a scene.

blocks.title: Why good people freeze
blocks.body: The freeze is not a character flaw — it is predictable psychology. When others are present, responsibility diffuses: the more bystanders, the less likely any single one acts. Add social pressure ("don't be that person"), fear of misreading the situation, and not knowing what to actually say, and you get a quad full of people watching a friend slump against a wall. Naming these forces in advance is half the battle. If you expect the freeze, you can plan around it.

blocks.alt: Group of college students gathered closely at a social event
blocks.caption: Crowds dilute responsibility. The fix is to make one person — you — the someone.

items.title: Notice
items.body: Catch the signal early — the friend who's stumbling, the drink being pushed, the person getting walked upstairs. Look up from your phone.

items.title: Interpret
items.body: Name it as a problem, not 'just college.' If part of you feels uneasy, treat that as data, not drama.

items.title: Take responsibility
items.body: Decide it's yours to act on. Don't scan the room for a braver person — that scan is the diffusion trap.

blocks.title: Why students say they didn't step in
blocks.note: Illustrative figures for teaching the diffusion and skills gap — not from a specific study.

blocks.title: Know how, then act
blocks.body: The last two steps are where most training stops short. "Know how" means having a script loaded before you need it, so you're not composing words while a situation escalates. "Act" means choosing the lowest-friction move that works: the three classic options are direct, distract, and delegate. Direct is the head-on intervention. Distract pulls someone out of the moment without confrontation — "Hey, your roommate's looking for you." Delegate hands it to someone with more standing: the RA, the party host, campus safety. You don't have to be a hero. You have to be the one who does one of these.

blocks.text: The students who intervene aren't braver than the rest. They've just rehearsed the first sentence.

blocks.title: Red flags — stop watching and act now
items: Can't be woken, or wakes only briefly and slumps back down
Vomiting while passed out or unable to sit up on their own
Cold, clammy, or pale/bluish skin; slow or irregular breathing
Someone being steered toward a bedroom who clearly can't consent
A drink being pressed on someone who's already obviously impaired

blocks.title: The scripts that don't make a scene
blocks.body: Low-friction is the whole point — a quiet line beats a loud confrontation that nobody acts on. Use the distract move first: "Come help me find my charger," or "Let's get some water, I'm starving." To check on someone, skip the interrogation: "You good? Want to sit down for a sec?" To delegate, be specific and direct — vague calls for help get ignored. Don't shout "someone help!" to a crowd; point at one person: "You in the blue hoodie, grab the RA, I'll stay with her." Naming a single person defeats diffusion in real time.

blocks.alt: Two students talking quietly and supportively, one checking on the other
blocks.caption: Distract and check-in scripts let you intervene without an audience or a confrontation.

items.body: Look up and clock the signal early — before it becomes a crisis.
Trust the unease. Decide whether this needs a check-in or a call.
Make yourself the someone. Don't wait for a braver bystander.
Direct, distract, or delegate — choose the lowest-friction one that works.
If it's a real medical risk, call for help and don't leave them alone.

blocks.title: In the moment, in order
Being an ally is a decision, not a personality
blocks.body: You won't feel brave in the moment — nobody does. The students who step in aren't a different breed; they've simply decided ahead of time that they're the type who acts, and they've got a sentence ready. Most campuses also have a medical amnesty or Good Samaritan policy precisely so that fear of getting in trouble never costs someone their safety. Notice, interpret, own it, know how, act. Carry the frame in, and when the moment comes, you'll already know your first line.

blocks.title: The last decision of the night is the one that matters
blocks.body: Most of the night's risk doesn't show up at the pregame. It shows up at 1 a.m., in a parking lot, when someone is fishing for keys and insisting they're "fine to drive." By then the easy interventions are gone. What's left is a fast judgment call about who gets behind the wheel, who rides with whom, and who you don't let leave alone. "Getting home safe" is the part of the night people plan for least and need most. This lesson teaches you to make that call cleanly, even when the person arguing is your roommate, your ride, or you.

blocks.title: "I'm fine" is data, not a verdict
blocks.body: The driver who feels fine is the most dangerous one, because alcohol impairs the exact judgment they're using to rate themselves. Coordination, reaction time, and risk perception drop well before someone looks or sounds drunk, and they recover on alcohol's schedule, not on coffee, a cold shower, or a 20-minute nap. You can't sober someone up faster; you can only keep them out of the driver's seat until time does it. So treat "I'm fine" as one input among many, and weight what you actually saw them drink far more heavily than how they're presenting right now.

blocks.alt: A set of car keys resting on a table at night
blocks.caption: Taking the keys is the simplest intervention you have. Make it the default, not the last resort.

items.title: Keys
items.body: Move them early and quietly. A driver who can't find their keys rarely escalates the way one you openly confront does. Pocket them, hand them to a sober friend, or 'hold' them while you sort the ride.

items.title: Rides
items.body: Have the backup ready before it's needed: rideshare, a sober designated driver, a campus safe-ride or escort line, or a friend you can text. A plan made sober beats one negotiated at 1 a.m.

items.title: Handoffs
items.body: Don't let an impaired person leave alone or into a stranger's car. Get them to a known, sober person and confirm the handoff happened — a text back, not an assumption.

blocks.title: How students who got home safely actually got there
blocks.note: Illustrative figures for teaching purposes, not from a specific survey.

blocks.text: The students we lose almost never planned to drive drunk. They planned nothing — and at 1 a.m., no plan defaults to the car.

blocks.title: Red flags — do not let them drive, and don't let them leave alone
items: Slurred speech, stumbling, or trouble standing without support
Can't track the conversation, repeats themselves, or seems confused about where they are
You watched them take shots or lose count — your eyes outrank their self-report
Vomiting, then saying they feel 'better' and ready to go
Getting into a car with people they don't know, or wandering off solo

blocks.title: Make the call without making it a fight
blocks.body: Confrontation triggers defensiveness, so lower the stakes instead of raising them. Don't debate whether they're drunk — give them an easier option than driving. "My phone's already got the app open, let's just split a ride" or "crash here, deal with the car in the morning" lets someone say yes without admitting they were wrong. Use the group: a second person nodding along does more than you arguing alone. And if they push past all of it and head for the car anyway, you've still got the keys you moved twenty minutes ago — which is exactly why you moved them then instead of now.

blocks.alt: Friends walking together down a city street at night
blocks.caption: A handoff isn't done until someone safe has them. Walk them to the door, then confirm.

blocks.title: Where handoffs quietly fail
blocks.body: The common mistake isn't refusing to help — it's a sloppy handoff. You put someone in a rideshare but never confirm they got home. You assume their roommate is awake. You let them 'walk it off' alone because they seemed steady at the door. An impaired person can deteriorate after you stop watching, especially if they keep drinking or were heavier than you realized. Close the loop: name who's responsible, hand off in person when you can, and get a confirmation back. 'Probably fine' is not a handoff.

items.lead: Read the person, not their words.
items.body: Weight what you saw them drink and how they're moving over their 'I'm fine.'
Move them early and quietly so driving stops being an option before it becomes an argument.
Have a ride ready — rideshare, sober friend, campus safe-ride — and frame it as the convenient choice.
Get a second voice on your side; don't try to win it alone.
Deliver them to a known sober person and get a text back that they're home and okay.

blocks.title: When the night winds down, run this
The bottom line
blocks.body: Safe-ride and handoff decisions reward the person who planned thirty minutes ago and stayed calm thirty seconds ago. You can't sober anyone up, you can't out-argue impaired judgment, and you can't undo a drive once it starts — but you can move a set of keys, open a rideshare app, and refuse to let someone leave alone. None of that requires being the loudest person in the parking lot. It just requires being the one who already decided how the night ends.

blocks.title: What to scan before you read
Read the source before you read the source
blocks.body: You don't have time to deep-read every article, page, and PDF a search throws at you. You don't have to. Before a single sentence of a source enters your notes or your draft, run a fast scan that asks four blunt questions: who wrote it, what are they citing, when was it published, and where did it appear? Thirty seconds, four signals. If all four come back clean, read on with normal skepticism. If any one is murky, your bar to use the source goes up — you keep looking, or you treat the claim as a lead to verify, not a fact to quote.

blocks.title: The four signals, and why they hold
blocks.body: Author tells you whether a human with relevant expertise stands behind the claim, or whether it's anonymous, a content mill, or someone outside their lane. Citations tell you whether the piece rests on evidence you can trace, or on assertion. Date matters because a 2009 statistic on, say, social-media use is a historical artifact, not current fact. Venue — a peer-reviewed journal, a university press, a newsroom with corrections, versus a personal blog or an SEO listicle — sets the baseline scrutiny each claim received before it reached you. None of the four is decisive alone. Together they tell you fast how hard the source worked to be right.

items.title: Who
items.body: Named author with a relevant role, affiliation, or track record — not 'Admin,' not a brand voice, not someone credentialed in an unrelated field.

items.title: What & When
items.body: Claims backed by traceable citations, and a publish or update date recent enough that the facts haven't moved on without it.

items.title: Where
items.body: A venue with editorial standards — peer review, an editor, a corrections policy — rather than an open platform where anyone posts unchecked.

blocks.title: What students actually check first (illustrative)

blocks.text: Students don't get fooled by bad sources. They get fooled by sources that look the part — clean design, confident tone — and never asked the four questions.

blocks.title: Red flags that raise your bar
items: No author named, or an author writing well outside their field
Strong claims with zero citations, or citations that only loop back to the same site
No date, or a date old enough that the facts have likely changed
A venue that exists to sell, rank, or persuade rather than to report or research
A title or framing engineered for clicks and outrage rather than accuracy

blocks.title: Murky isn't the same as worthless
blocks.body: A failed signal doesn't mean delete the tab. It means change how you use the source. A thinly sourced blog post can still point you toward the study it half-summarizes — chase that study and cite the original. A dated but authoritative report can anchor your background section as long as you flag its age. The mistake isn't using imperfect sources; it's letting an imperfect source pass as a settled fact in your draft without ever noticing the signal it failed.

blocks.title: The common trap: design as credibility
blocks.body: The fastest way to get burned is to let a polished site stand in for the four signals. Clean typography, a confident tone, and a top-three search ranking tell you a page was built well and optimized hard — not that it's accurate. Google ranks for relevance and authority signals, not truth. Run the scan anyway. The page that looks the most trustworthy is often the one counting on you not to check.

items.body: Look for a name and a role. No human, or the wrong kind of expertise? Flag it.
Are claims linked or footnoted to evidence you could trace? Or is it bare assertion?
Recent enough that the facts still hold? Old data needs a reason to still be relevant.
Journal, press, newsroom — or blog, forum, content mill? Set your scrutiny to match.
All four clean: read on. Any murky: keep looking, or verify the claim before you trust it.

blocks.title: The 30-second check, in order
Make it a reflex
blocks.body: The goal isn't to judge sources perfectly — it's to never let one into your draft unscanned. Done a few dozen times, the four questions stop being a checklist and become the way you read. You'll feel the murky ones in the first ten seconds, and you'll have raised your bar before you ever copied a word. That instinct, repeated across a whole research assignment, is the difference between a draft built on evidence and one built on whatever ranked first.

blocks.title: Bias is not a disqualifier
blocks.body: When you find out a source has a viewpoint, the temptation is to throw it out. Resist that. Every source — every researcher, journalist, think tank, and government agency — comes from somewhere. A study funded by a teachers' union and a report from a charter-school advocacy group can both contain solid data. The real question isn't whether the bias exists. It's whether it's disclosed, whether the evidence still holds when you read past the framing, and whether you can triangulate the claim against a source that wants the opposite to be true.

blocks.title: Disclosed bias is workable; hidden bias is the trap
blocks.body: A peer-reviewed article that names its funding source, states its limitations, and links its dataset is being honest with you about where it stands. You can account for that. The dangerous source is the one that hides its angle behind a neutral-sounding name or a .org domain — an 'institute' that turns out to be a single advocacy donor, a 'study' with no methods section. Disclosure isn't proof of truth, but concealment is a reliable warning sign. Look for who paid, who wrote, and what they chose not to mention.

items.title: Disclosure
items.body: Is the funding, affiliation, or stance stated up front? Named bias is bias you can adjust for. Hidden bias contaminates everything downstream.

items.title: Evidence
items.body: Strip the framing. Do the numbers, sample size, and methods still support the claim, or only the spin around it?

items.title: Triangulation
items.body: Can you confirm the core finding in a source with the opposite incentive? Agreement across rivals is the strongest signal you have.

blocks.title: Read the methods, not just the conclusion
blocks.body: Bias lives in the method long before it reaches the conclusion. A survey of 80 self-selected respondents and a randomized study of 8,000 students can reach the same headline — but they are not the same evidence. Check the sample size, how subjects were chosen, whether there was a control group, and whether the author measured what they claim to measure. A strong method survives a hostile reading. A weak one only works if you already agree with it.

blocks.title: How often a claim survives a hostile re-read, by source signal
blocks.note: Illustrative figures to show the pattern, not measured research data.

blocks.text: I don't trust the source that has no opinion. I trust the one that shows its work and tells me who's paying for the lab.

blocks.title: Red flags that turn bias into disqualification
items: No methods section — a strong claim with no description of how it was reached
Funder and finding line up perfectly, with no acknowledged limitations
A neutral-sounding name ('Center for…', 'Institute of…') with no listed authors or board
The same statistic recycled across many sites that all trace back to one unsourced original
Emotional framing doing the work that evidence should be doing

blocks.title: The common mistake: confusing tone with rigor
blocks.body: Students often reject a source because it sounds opinionated and accept one because it sounds calm and academic. Tone is not evidence. A passionately argued op-ed can rest on solid data, and a measured-sounding report can be built on a rigged sample. Judge the support beneath the sentence, not the temperature of the sentence itself. The goal of this lesson isn't to find the one unbiased source — it doesn't exist — it's to build a balanced set of biased sources whose evidence converges.

items.body: Identify who wrote it, who funded it, and what outcome would benefit them.
Is that stance stated openly, or did you have to dig for it? Hidden is a strike.
Read the sample size, selection, and measures. Decide if the evidence holds without the framing.
Find the same core finding in a source with an opposing incentive before you cite it.
Keep it with its bias noted, balance it with a counter-view, or drop it if the evidence collapses.

blocks.title: Vet a biased source in order
The takeaway
blocks.body: You will never assemble a draft from sources that have no point of view. What you can do is choose sources that are honest about their angle, sturdy in their evidence, and confirmable against their rivals. Bias tells you where a source is standing. Methodology tells you whether to listen. Triangulation tells you whether it's true. Use all three — and bias stops being a reason to discard and becomes a thing you can simply account for.

blocks.title: You already know this. Here's the fast reload.
blocks.body: Your prior practice showed strong source-evaluation instincts, so this lesson is a checkpoint, not a tutorial. Skim it, confirm nothing has gone rusty, and move on. The reason it sits at the front of the course is structural: every later module — building a working bibliography, defending a methodology, synthesizing a literature base — assumes you can size up a source in under a minute and trust your own verdict. If that reflex is solid, the rest of the term paper becomes a planning problem, not a sorting problem. Read this to make sure the floor under you holds.

blocks.title: Credibility is contextual, not absolute
blocks.body: A source is not 'good' or 'bad' in a vacuum — it is fit or unfit for the claim you are making. A 2014 conference abstract is weak evidence for a current statistic but perfectly credible as a marker of when a debate emerged. A trade magazine is a poor authority on mechanism but a strong one on industry practice. At the upper-division level, your reader assumes you can hold both the source's reliability and its relevance to your specific argument in view at once. The fast question is never 'Is this credible?' — it is 'Credible for what, in this paragraph?'

items.title: Authority
items.body: Who produced this, and what gives them standing on this exact claim? Credentials, institutional affiliation, and a track record in the relevant subfield — not general fame.

items.title: Evidence
items.body: Are claims backed by data, citations, or method you can trace? Peer review and a reference list signal accountability. Assertion without a trail is opinion.

items.title: Purpose
items.body: Why does this exist — to inform, persuade, sell, or advocate? Funding, sponsorship, and intended audience shape what gets emphasized and what gets buried.

blocks.note: Illustrative target mix for a term paper's cited base — not a fixed quota. Your discipline and prompt will shift these weights.

blocks.text: Students lose points not for citing a weak source, but for citing it as if it were a strong one.
